q.prompt: How old is the writer now?

captions: Hello, and welcome to Camday English, Stage 9. In this lesson: The year 2075.
Use future continuous and future perfect to make predictions.
Here are some new words. Prediction. A statement about what will happen. Sustainable.
Able to continue without damaging the environment. Artificial intelligence.
Computer systems that can do tasks that need human thinking.
And some more words. Automated. Done by machines without people. Population.
The number of people living in a place. Transform. Change completely.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: a statement about what will happen?
Now some grammar: Future continuous and future perfect.
The future continuous, will be plus the i n g form, is for an action in progress at a future time.
The future perfect, will have plus past participle, is for an action completed before a future time.
For example: In 2075, people will be living in floating cities.
For example: By 2075, scientists will have found new energy sources.
Now listen, and read along. A letter to 2075.
Dear reader in 2075, I am writing this in 2026, and I am thirteen years old.
By the time you read this, I will have turned sixty-two. I wonder what your world looks like.
Maybe you will be living in a city that floats on the sea, as some engineers already predict.
Maybe your car will be driving itself, while you read or sleep.
Perhaps artificial intelligence will have transformed almost every job,
and people will be working only three days a week.
I hope that by 2075 we will have found sustainable ways to produce energy and food for a population of nearly ten billion people.
I hope that the coral reefs will still be there.
Please don't judge us too harshly for the mistakes we made.
We knew some things were wrong, and many of us were trying to change them. With hope, A student from 2026
Another question. The video will stop. How old is the writer now?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like prediction, sustainable, artificial intelligence.
You practised future continuous and future perfect. And you read A letter to 2075.
Now try the practice questions. See you next time!

captions: Hello, and welcome to Camday English, Stage 9. In this lesson: Should we live on Mars?
Discuss possibilities and give balanced opinions using a range of modal and hedging language.
Here are some new words. Colony. A group of people living in a new place far from home. Ethical.
To do with what is morally right or wrong. Resources.
Things such as money, water and energy that can be used.
And some more words. Priority. Something that is more important than other things. Feasible.
Possible and likely to work. Hostile. Very unfriendly or difficult to live in.
Time for a question. The video will stop.
Which word means: a group of people living in a new place far from home?
Now some grammar: Expressing degrees of certainty.
Use a range of language from certain to unlikely: will definitely, is likely to, may well, could possibly,
is unlikely to, definitely won't. For example: Humans are likely to visit Mars within 20 years.
For example: A large Mars colony is unlikely to exist before 2100.
Now listen, and read along. Mars: a new home or an expensive dream?
Ever since the first robots landed on Mars, people have asked whether humans could one day live there.
Supporters argue that building a colony on another planet may well be necessary for humanity's long-term survival.
They also point out that space research has already led to useful inventions on Earth,
from water filters to better medical scanners. However, Mars is an extremely hostile place.
It has almost no oxygen, temperatures can fall below minus 100 degrees,
and the surface is exposed to dangerous radiation. Many scientists believe that a large,
self-sufficient colony is unlikely to be feasible for at least a hundred years.
Others raise ethical questions. With so many problems on Earth – climate change, hunger,
disease – should we spend enormous resources on another planet?
Shouldn't our first priority be to look after the only home we know?
Perhaps the answer lies somewhere in between: continue exploring, but never treat Mars as a ‘Planet B’.
As one engineer put it, ‘There is no Planet B – but there is a lot we can learn by trying to build one.’
Another question. The video will stop. Why do supporters think a Mars colony may be necessary?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like colony, ethical, resources.
You practised expressing degrees of certainty. And you read Mars: a new home or an expensive dream?
Now try the practice questions. See you next time!

Mars: a new home or an expensive dream?
Ever since the first robots landed on Mars, people have asked whether humans could one day live there.
Supporters argue that building a colony on another planet may well be necessary for humanity's long-term survival. They also point out that space research has already led to useful inventions on Earth, from water filters to better medical scanners.
However, Mars is an extremely hostile place. It has almost no oxygen, temperatures can fall below minus 100 degrees, and the surface is exposed to dangerous radiation. Many scientists believe that a large, self-sufficient colony is unlikely to be feasible for at least a hundred years.
Others raise ethical questions. With so many problems on Earth – climate change, hunger, disease – should we spend enormous resources on another planet? Shouldn't our first priority be to look after the only home we know?
Perhaps the answer lies somewhere in between: continue exploring, but never treat Mars as a ‘Planet B’. As one engineer put it, ‘There is no Planet B – but there is a lot we can learn by trying to build one.’

options.t: Continue exploring, but don't treat Mars as a ‘Planet B’.

A.ctx:
A letter to 2075
Dear reader in 2075,
I am writing this in 2026, and I am thirteen years old. By the time you read this, I will have turned sixty-two. I wonder what your world looks like.
Maybe you will be living in a city that floats on the sea, as some engineers already predict. Maybe your car will be driving itself, while you read or sleep. Perhaps artificial intelligence will have transformed almost every job, and people will be working only three days a week.
I hope that by 2075 we will have found sustainable ways to produce energy and food for a population of nearly ten billion people. I hope that the coral reefs will still be there.
Please don't judge us too harshly for the mistakes we made. We knew some things were wrong, and many of us were trying to change them.
With hope,
A student from 2026
